export const meta = {
  name: 'pkp-validator-and-ross',
  description: 'Reimplement Extron\'s driver validator in pure Python and analyse a hand-authored ControlScript module set',
  phases: [
    { title: 'Decode' },
    { title: 'Ross' },
    { title: 'Implement' },
    { title: 'Verify' },
  ],
}

const REPO = 'Z:\\GitHub\\rob-paprocki\\extron-driver-convert'
const GCP = 'C:\\Program Files (x86)\\Extron\\GCP'

const CONTEXT = `
CONTEXT — repo: ${REPO} (read CLAUDE.md and STATUS.md first; standard-library Python only, no deps).

Extron Global Configurator validates a .pkp before use:
  Extron.Configuration.Drivers.DriverAssetValidator.Validate(IDriverFileAsset) -> ErrorCode
  enum ErrorCode { Valid = 0, MismatchHash = 80085, NoHash_NoGuid = 80086 }
GC shows "Invalid Driver ... Error Code: 80085" when it fails.

Already MEASURED by the main session (do not re-derive, but DO challenge if you find contradicting evidence):
 - DriverFileAsset._resourceHashDict is Dictionary<string, byte[]>: resource key -> 32-byte digest.
   Its NRBF shape is {Version, Comparer, HashSize, KeyValuePairs}; KeyValuePairs is a BinaryArray of
   KeyValuePair<string,byte[]> entries with members "key" and "value".
 - The digest is plain SHA-256 over the resource bytes. Verified: sha256(donor script utf-8 bytes)
   == the stored digest cc80101d367ad0d13162ed0daee29b580155543d2fcd22449fa583a0d0505eb3.
 - ComputeHash's IL constructs SHA256CryptoServiceProvider and calls ComputeHash(stream).
 - Packages carry a hash per resource: the embedded .py AND the comm-sheet .pdf.
 - The .pdf hash cannot currently be checked from the object graph alone (the pdf is a separate
   resource) - determine whether it is embedded in the package or external. This matters.

Tools already in the repo:
 - tools/pkp_dump.py     NRBF reader (PkpParser, load_bytes). Parses all 1853 shipping packages, 0 errors.
 - tools/pkp_build.py    transplant builder; has resource_hashes() and refresh_resource_hash().
 - experiments/nrbf_writeback/nrbf_write.py  NRBF writer.
Run python as: python (it is on PATH).
`

const IL = `
DriverAssetValidator.Validate — IL 234 bytes, maxstack 3, locals:
  local[0] IEnumerator\`1   local[1] IResourceAsset   local[2] Byte[]   local[3] ErrorCode
IL bytes (hex):

08 28 1B 00 00 2B 2D 6D 2B 5B 06 6F F6 00 00 0A 0B 07 6F 99 00 00 0A 0C 03 6F FD 00 00 0A 07 6F 85
00 00 0A 6F 97 00 00 0A 2C 25 2B 00 03 6F FD 00 00 0A 07 6F 85 00 00 0A 6F FE 00 00 0A 08 28 1B 00
00 2B 2D 2F 2B 00 20 D5 38 01 00 0D DE 77 02 7B 23 00 00 04 07 6F F4 00 00 0A 6F F7 00 00 0A 2C 0A
2B 8A 20 D5 38 01 00 0D DE 5A 20 D6 38 01 00 0D DE 52 06 6F 60 00 00 0A 3A 8A FF FF FF 2B 00 DE 41
06 2C 0A 2B 00 06 6F 2E 00 00 0A 2B 00 DC 72 5C 06 00 70 73 FF 00 00 0A 7A 03 6F 86 00 00 0A 72 9C
06 00 70 19 6F 00 01 00 0A 2C 04 2B 00 16 2A 03 6F 8B 00 00 0A 6F F3 00 00 0A 0A 38 25 FF FF FF 16 2A 09 2A

ComputeHash — IL 49 bytes, locals: local[0] Byte[]  local[1] SHA256CryptoServiceProvider
14 0A 2B 00 73 F8 00 00 0A 0B 2B 00 07 03 6F F9 00 00 0A 0A 07 6F FA 00 00 0A DE 0E 07 2C 0A 2B 00
07 6F 2E 00 00 0A 2B 00 DC DE 03 26 FE 1A 06 2A

Note 0x000138D5 = 80085 and 0x000138D6 = 80086 appear as ldc.i4 operands.
You may inspect the assembly yourself with 32-bit Windows PowerShell:
  & "C:\\Windows\\SysWOW64\\WindowsPowerShell\\v1.0\\powershell.exe" -NoProfile -File <script.ps1>
loading ${GCP}\\Extron.Configuration.Drivers.dll via [Reflection.Assembly]::LoadFrom.
Resolve metadata tokens (0x0A000xxx = MemberRef, 0x04000023 = Field) via Module.ResolveMember to name
the actual calls rather than guessing. That is the difference between a spec and a story.
`

const SPEC_SCHEMA = {
  type: 'object',
  properties: {
    pseudocode: { type: 'string', description: 'Faithful pseudocode of Validate(), control flow exact' },
    resolved_calls: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'string' },
      description: 'metadata token -> resolved member name, one per line, for every call site you resolved' },
    returns_valid_when: { type: 'string' },
    returns_mismatchhash_when: { type: 'string' },
    returns_nohash_noguid_when: { type: 'string' },
    which_resources_are_hashed: { type: 'string',
      description: 'Exactly which resources are iterated and hashed, and any filtering (e.g. extension checks)' },
    string_literals: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'string' },
      description: 'ldstr literals referenced by the method, resolved' },
    uncertainties: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'string' },
      description: 'Anything you could NOT resolve. Be explicit; do not paper over.' },
    confidence: { type: 'string', enum: ['high', 'medium', 'low'] },
  },
  required: ['pseudocode', 'returns_valid_when', 'returns_mismatchhash_when',
             'returns_nohash_noguid_when', 'which_resources_are_hashed', 'uncertainties', 'confidence'],
}

phase('Decode')
const decodes = await parallel([0, 1, 2].map(i => () => agent(
  `${CONTEXT}\n${IL}\n\nTASK: decode DriverAssetValidator.Validate into faithful pseudocode.\n` +
  `Resolve the metadata tokens to real member names using reflection (Module.ResolveMember /\n` +
  `ResolveString) rather than inferring from opcode shape. State precisely under which conditions\n` +
  `each of the three ErrorCode values is returned, and exactly which resources get hashed —\n` +
  `note the ldstr + EndsWith-looking sequence near the end, it may filter by file extension.\n` +
  `Attempt ${i + 1} of 3, independent — do not assume the other attempts exist.\n` +
  `Report what you could not resolve in 'uncertainties'. An honest gap beats a confident guess.`,
  { label: `decode-il-${i + 1}`, phase: 'Decode', schema: SPEC_SCHEMA, effort: 'high' })))

const ROSS_FILES = [
  { f: 'mod_ross_matrix_RossTalk_v1_1_0_0.py', what: 'hand-authored ControlScript device module (RossTalk protocol)' },
  { f: 'mod_ross_matrix_tsl_3_1_v1_1_0_0.py', what: 'hand-authored ControlScript device module (TSL 3.1 protocol)' },
  { f: 'plugin_ross_ultrix.py', what: 'a plugin/translation layer above the two device modules' },
  { f: 'tools.py', what: 'a ~398KB shared framework the programmer wrote (36 top-level classes/functions)' },
]

phase('Ross')
const ross = await parallel(ROSS_FILES.map(r => () => agent(
  `${CONTEXT}\n\nTASK: analyse samples/Custom Module/${r.f} — ${r.what}.\n\n` +
  `This material is NEW to the repo: modules a third-party programmer hand-wrote for Ross Ultrix,\n` +
  `a device Extron does not ship a driver for. Every other ControlScript module in this repo was\n` +
  `generated by Extron's own tooling. So this is the first evidence of what a HUMAN writes when\n` +
  `targeting an unsupported API, and the project's live question is exactly that: how to author a\n` +
  `driver for hardware the vendor does not support (see findings/13, the Crestron 1 Beyond i20).\n\n` +
  `Answer concretely, with line references:\n` +
  ` 1. Structure vs Extron's generated modules (DeviceClass, self.Commands, __SetHelper/__UpdateHelper,\n` +
  `    SubscribeStatus/NewStatus/WriteStatus/ReadStatus, the three transport classes). What conforms,\n` +
  `    what deviates, and does any deviation look deliberate rather than sloppy?\n` +
  ` 2. What does the author do that Extron's generator does NOT, and vice versa?\n` +
  ` 3. Does tools/wire_table.py extract a wire table from it? RUN IT:\n` +
  `      python -c "import sys; sys.path.insert(0,'tools'); import wire_table; ` +
  `t=wire_table.extract_table(open(r'samples/Custom Module/${r.f}',encoding='utf-8').read(),'${r.f}'); ` +
  `print(len(t.commands), sorted(t.commands))"\n` +
  `    If it fails or under-extracts, say exactly how. Our oracle has only ever been run on\n` +
  `    machine-generated modules; this is its first hand-written input.\n` +
  ` 4. Anything reusable for authoring the i20 driver, or that contradicts our assumptions.\n` +
  `For tools.py, do NOT read all 398KB — map its top-level classes and report what the framework\n` +
  `provides, then read only what matters.\n\n` +
  `Return prose with concrete file:line citations. No summary padding.`,
  { label: `ross:${r.f.replace(/\.py$/, '')}`, phase: 'Ross', effort: 'high' })))

phase('Implement')
const spec = decodes.filter(Boolean)
const implementation = await agent(
  `${CONTEXT}\n\nThree independent decodes of DriverAssetValidator.Validate:\n\n` +
  spec.map((s, i) => `--- decode ${i + 1} (confidence: ${s.confidence}) ---\n` +
    `pseudocode:\n${s.pseudocode}\n` +
    `Valid when: ${s.returns_valid_when}\n` +
    `MismatchHash when: ${s.returns_mismatchhash_when}\n` +
    `NoHash_NoGuid when: ${s.returns_nohash_noguid_when}\n` +
    `resources hashed: ${s.which_resources_are_hashed}\n` +
    `uncertainties: ${(s.uncertainties || []).join('; ')}\n`).join('\n') +
  `\n\nTASK: write tools/pkp_validate.py — a PURE PYTHON (standard library only) reimplementation of\n` +
  `Extron's validator, so this repo can check a package on any machine WITHOUT Global Configurator\n` +
  `installed. That is the whole point: GC is Windows-only and licensed; the repo is cloud-first.\n\n` +
  `Requirements:\n` +
  ` - Reuse tools/pkp_dump.py to parse; do not write a second NRBF reader.\n` +
  ` - Public API: validate(path_or_bytes) -> Result with .code (int), .name (str), .details.\n` +
  `   Mirror Extron's enum exactly: Valid=0, MismatchHash=80085, NoHash_NoGuid=80086.\n` +
  ` - CLI: python tools/pkp_validate.py FILE... printing one line per package, non-zero exit if any invalid.\n` +
  ` - Where the three decodes DISAGREE, or a decode listed an uncertainty, implement the behaviour you\n` +
  `   can justify from evidence and record the disagreement in a module-level comment. Do NOT silently\n` +
  `   pick one. This repo's standing rule: a plausible guess is worse than a recorded gap.\n` +
  ` - Handle the .pdf resource honestly: if its bytes are not in the package, you cannot verify its\n` +
  `   hash — say so in the Result rather than pretending it passed.\n\n` +
  `Also write tools/test_pkp_validate.py in the SAME style as tools/test_pkp_build.py (plain script,\n` +
  `no pytest, prints "N passed, M failed"). It must cover: every sample package validates Valid;\n` +
  `a script mutated WITHOUT a hash refresh returns MismatchHash; the same mutation WITH\n` +
  `pkp_build.refresh_resource_hash returns Valid; and a truncated/garbage input fails loudly rather\n` +
  `than returning Valid.\n\n` +
  `Run both files before you finish. Report the final test output verbatim.`,
  { label: 'write-pkp-validate', phase: 'Implement', effort: 'high' })

phase('Verify')
const checks = [
  ['differential', `Differentially test tools/pkp_validate.py against Extron's REAL validator over a large sample.\n` +
    `Extron's validator, via 32-bit Windows PowerShell (the DLL is x86 .NET Framework):\n` +
    `  [Reflection.Assembly]::LoadFrom("${GCP}\\Extron.Configuration.Contracts.dll")\n` +
    `  [Reflection.Assembly]::LoadFrom("${GCP}\\Extron.Configuration.Core.dll")\n` +
    `  $asm=[Reflection.Assembly]::LoadFrom("${GCP}\\Extron.Configuration.Drivers.dll")\n` +
    `  DriverFileAsset.LoadFromFile(string) then DriverAssetValidator.Instance.Validate(asset)\n` +
    `  (marshal args as explicit object[] with [string] casts, or PowerShell boxes them and Invoke throws)\n` +
    `Run BOTH validators over at least 300 packages from C:\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\extron\\Driver3\n` +
    `plus every .pkp under ${REPO}\\samples and ${REPO}\\experiments\\skeleton_i20\\out.\n` +
    `Report: total compared, exact agreements, and EVERY disagreement with the package name and both\n` +
    `verdicts. A disagreement is the most valuable thing you can find - hunt for one.`],
  ['adversarial', `Adversarially review tools/pkp_validate.py. Try to REFUTE that it faithfully reimplements\n` +
    `Extron's validator. Specifically hunt for: a package it calls Valid that Extron would reject;\n` +
    `reliance on a field that is absent in some real packages; mishandling of the .pdf resource;\n` +
    `an exception path that returns Valid by accident; and any case where it silently guesses rather\n` +
    `than recording a gap. Construct concrete counterexample packages with tools/pkp_build.py and\n` +
    `TEST them against both validators. Report each attempted refutation and whether it succeeded.`],
  ['integration', `Check that tools/pkp_validate.py is genuinely usable without Global Configurator, which is\n` +
    `its entire purpose. Verify: standard library only (no imports outside stdlib + repo modules);\n` +
    `no path under "Program Files" or any GC-installed file referenced at runtime; works from a\n` +
    `different working directory; the CLI exits non-zero on an invalid package. Then run the repo's\n` +
    `whole existing suite (tools/test_pkp2cs.py, test_wire_table.py, test_pkg_dump.py,\n` +
    `test_pkp_build.py, experiments/nrbf_writeback/test_nrbf_write.py,\n` +
    `experiments/crestron2cs/test_crestron2cs.py, experiments/skeleton_i20/test_i20_wire.py,\n` +
    `experiments/skeleton_i20/test_i20_cs_wire.py) and confirm nothing regressed. Report each\n` +
    `suite's final line verbatim.`],
]
const verdicts = await parallel(checks.map(([label, task]) => () => agent(
  `${CONTEXT}\n\nThe implementer reported:\n${String(implementation).slice(0, 3000)}\n\nTASK: ${task}`,
  { label: `verify:${label}`, phase: 'Verify', effort: 'high' })))

return {
  decodes: spec.map(s => ({ confidence: s.confidence, uncertainties: s.uncertainties })),
  implementation: String(implementation).slice(0, 4000),
  verdicts: verdicts.filter(Boolean).map(String),
  ross: ross.filter(Boolean).map(String),
}

uncertainties: I did not pin down the exact call site of DriverAssetValidator.LoadDefaultFromResource() inside GCP.exe. I proved GCP.exe carries MemberRefs to DriverAssetValidator.Instance, .LoadDefaultFromResource and .Validate (tokens 0x0A000D94/D95/D96), and Extron.Configuration.GCPro.dll carries .Instance and .Validate (0x0A0008E8/E9). MemberRef rows only exist when referenced, so the calls almost certainly exist, but my IL-scan over those two assemblies returned no USE hits (their types load only partially via ReflectionTypeLoadException and the recovered Type objects gave no method bodies). So: WHETHER the Guid table `this.a` is non-empty at the moment GC calls Validate is inferred, not measured. If it were never loaded, the fallback branch would always miss and the 'unknown resource' outcome would always be 80086.

I could not determine which validator instance the callers use in each case. Both callers reference the static singleton `DriverAssetValidator.Instance`; the instance .ctor sets `a = new Dictionary<Guid,byte[]>()` and does NOT call LoadDefaultFromResource, so population is entirely up to the caller.

The `Filename` used by the 'eir' test: I verified the .pkp loader `DriverFileAsset.cq` sets `asset.Filename = Path.GetFileName(fi.FullName)` and `DriverFileAsset.Load(string)` calls set_Filename before throwing NotImplementedException. I did NOT verify every code path that can produce an IDriverFileAsset (notably CachedDriverFileAsset and whatever GC's 61 MB catalogue rehydrates) also overwrites Filename. In the raw NRBF of all 9 sample packages the stored `DriverDescriptorAsset+_filename` is the AUTHORING absolute path (e.g. 'C:\\Users\\billywong\\OneDrive - Extron\\Desktop\\pakage holding folder\\extr_17_17677_v1_0_0.pkp'), which still ends in 'pkp', so the bypass does not fire either way for these — but the general claim 'Filename is always the on-disk name' is unproven.

The literal is "eir" with no leading dot and InvariantCultureIgnoreCase, so any Filename ending in those three characters bypasses validation. I have NOT tested whether a reachable load path can hand Validate an asset whose Filename ends in 'eir' while the file is actually a .pkp — that would be a validation bypass, but it is speculation until someone drives it.

GetContentHashCode() returns null when Content is not a byte[] (ResourceAssetBase.GetContentHashCode does `Content as byte[]` then ComputeHashBySHA256Cypto, which returns null for null and swallows exceptions). Validate has a try/FINALLY only, no catch, so a null hash reaching Enumerable.SequenceEqual would throw ArgumentNullException out of Validate rather than returning an ErrorCode. Same for a null value stored in either dictionary. I did not observe this in practice — every resource in all 9 sample packages has byte[] content.

I did not decode DriverFileAsset.get_Manifest()'s body in full (it is a LINQ projection over the asset's child collection). I therefore rely on the object graph rather than the IL for the claim that the manifest's members are exactly the StreamResourceAsset children. If get_Manifest filters or synthesises entries, the hashed set could differ from the two/three StreamResourceAssets I enumerated.

Nothing in Extron.Configuration.Drivers.dll calls DriverAssetValidator.ComputeHash(Stream). It may be dead code or called from another assembly; I only scanned this DLL for its callers. Either way it is NOT on Validate's path.

ExtronDH.dat's 4,775 Guid keys matched NONE of the 21 resource GUIDs (or 9 root GUIDs) across the 9 sample packages. I did not determine what those 4,775 GUIDs actually key — plausibly legacy packages that predate _resourceHashDict, but that is a guess. I extracted the file to C:\\Users\\robp\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\ilres\\ExtronDH.dat if the parent wants to check it against the 6,644-package library.

Where field 'a' is populated in the real GC call path. Validate reads it unconditionally on the fallback branch. If the caller never invoked LoadDefaultFromResource()/Load(), 'a' is null and the `this.a.ContainsKey(r.Guid)` at IL 0x007D throws NullReferenceException instead of returning 80086. I did not trace GC's callers of DriverAssetValidator, so I cannot say whether the shipped ExtronDH.dat table is always loaded before Validate runs. This matters: it decides whether an unknown-Guid, unknown-key resource yields 80086 or an unhandled NRE.

I did not decode ExtronDH.dat itself (Load(Stream) deserializes it through what looks like a BinaryFormatter/obfuscated path at token 0x1B000028). So I do not know how many Guids it covers, nor whether third-party package resource Guids appear in it. That governs how often the fallback branch is live in practice.

GetContentHashCode returns null when Content is not a byte[] (`isinst Byte[]` -> null -> ComputeHashBySHA256Cypto returns null). Validate then passes null into Enumerable.SequenceEqual, which throws ArgumentNullException — Validate has only a finally, no catch, so that would propagate. I did not find a package where this occurs (all measured resources are byte[]), so this is read from IL, not observed.

StreamResourceAsset declares no override of GetContentHashCode/get_Content/get_Key, so I attribute all three to ResourceAssetBase. I verified this only with DeclaredOnly reflection on those specific names; an override under a different name reached through some other virtual slot would not have shown up.

`asset.Filename` for the EndsWith test: in the four packages I inspected it is the .pkp authoring path, so the test is false and hashing proceeds. I did not obtain an actual .eir asset to confirm that IDriverFileAsset is the type GC hands Validate for IR drivers, or that its Filename ends in "eir". The bypass is certain in the IL; its real-world trigger is inferred from the literal.

I checked 4 sample packages (DSC 12G-HD, Tesira, Samsung, plus root/manifest shape) — not the 1,853-package corpus. The claim "manifest = the .py files plus one .pdf, all embedded as byte[]" is measured on those; I did not verify no shipping package carries a resource type with non-byte[] content or a null _key.

IL offset 0x0010..0x002A is a shared compare block that the decompiler-style pseudocode duplicates into the Guid branch. It is reachable ONLY from the br.s at 0x0084, which I verified by disassembling all branch targets; there is no other predecessor. If some later analysis finds another entry, the else-branch reading changes.

The assembly is obfuscated (methods named a, b, cn; control flow padded with `br.s +0` and a br into the middle of the try region). I read the IL directly and cross-checked every branch target with my own disassembler, but I did not run a decompiler such as ILSpy/dnSpy to corroborate.

I did not observe an actual .eir-backed IDriverFileAsset flowing through Validate at runtime. I confirmed statically that the literal is the bare string "eir", that it is compared against IDriverDescriptorAsset.Filename with StringComparison.InvariantCultureIgnoreCase, and that a true result returns Valid before the manifest is touched. I did NOT confirm that Extron's .eir IR files are loaded as IDriverFileAsset instances with Filename ending in "eir" — that is a plausible inference, not a measurement. (For reference, the shipping .pkp files' Filename member is e.g. '1bynd_42_4279_v1_0_11.pkp', so Filename does carry the extension.)

CONTRADICTS STATUS.md: STATUS.md / CLAUDE.md state the GC driver library is '6,644 .pkp + 1,745 .eir'. Measured today at C:\Users\Public\Documents\extron\driver3 (recursive, no subdirectories): 1,853 .pkp and 26 .eir. The 1,853 figure agrees with this task's own prompt ('parses all 1853 shipping packages'), so the 6,644/1,745 numbers in STATUS.md look stale or refer to a different location/state. Flagging rather than silently reconciling.

Whether 80086 is reachable in practice for a normal package is an inference from two measurements, not a direct observation: (a) LoadDefaultFromResource is called only from GCPro.Services.DriverValidationService..ctor, and (b) none of the 19 sampled resource GUIDs or digests appear in ExtronDH.dat's 4,775 entries. I sampled 9 of 1,853 packages, not all of them. I also did not confirm that DriverValidationService is actually constructed in every code path that reaches Validate (DriverPortConfigurationValidationBuilder::e reads DriverAssetValidator.Instance directly, and if no DriverValidationService has been constructed at that point, `a` would still be empty).

Edge case not exercised: if a manifest resource's Content is not a byte[], ResourceAssetBase.GetContentHashCode() returns null, and Validate would pass null into Enumerable.SequenceEqual<byte>, which throws ArgumentNullException rather than returning an ErrorCode. Validate has no null check on local[2]. Every StreamResourceAsset I inspected had byte[] content, so I never saw this fire.

Validate does not null-check `iDriverFileAsset.Manifest` before calling GetEnumerator(). Because get_Manifest() auto-creates an empty AssetBase<IResourceAsset> when absent, this should not NRE in practice, but I inferred that from get_Manifest's IL (it calls DriverFileAsset.cn to attach the new child) rather than executing it. A DriverFileAsset that has been deserialized but not Load()ed would then present an empty manifest and validate as Valid — I did not test this and it is a meaningful claim I am deliberately not asserting.

At the project-level caller GCPro.Services.DriverValidationService.Validate(IGCProProjectAsset, bool), the aggregated failure dialog hardcodes `ldc.i4 80085` (boxed as ErrorCode) into Msg_InvalidDriver's {1} regardless of the actual code returned per driver. So a user-visible 'Error Code: 80085' from the project-level path is NOT proof that Validate returned MismatchHash rather than NoHash_NoGuid. Only the single-driver overload formats the real value. I did not determine which of the two paths produced the 80085 the project observed on hardware.

The `a` field name is the obfuscated/compiler-mangled member name as it appears in metadata; DriverAssetValidator's members are heavily renamed (a, b, cn, etc.). I report the resolved names exactly as Module.ResolveMember returned them and have not tried to recover original source names.

ProcessDriverDirectory uses Directory.GetFiles(dir, "*.pkp") and builds the Guid->hash map by calling ComputeHash(Stream) over whole .pkp FILES keyed by the DriverFileAsset's own Guid — I decoded its call graph (ProcessDriverDirectory -> a -> b) but did not fully decode method `b`'s IL, so my statement that ExtronDH.dat's keys are per-RESOURCE GUIDs versus per-PACKAGE GUIDs is not settled. Method b's resolved calls (get_Manifest, get_Current, get_Guid, IDictionary<Guid,byte[]>.Add, GetContentHashCode) point to per-resource, which would make the failed GUID lookups above expected rather than surprising, but I did not confirm it.

Both files written and run.

**Files (absolute paths)**
- `Z:\GitHub\rob-paprocki\extron-driver-convert\tools\pkp_validate.py` — pure-stdlib reimplementation of `DriverAssetValidator.Validate`, parsing delegated to `tools/pkp_dump.py` (no second NRBF reader).
- `Z:\GitHub\rob-paprocki\extron-driver-convert\tools\test_pkp_validate.py` — plain-script test suite in `test_pkp_build.py`'s style.

**API**: `validate(path_or_bytes, guid_hash_table=None, on_disk_name=None) -> Result` (`.code` / `.name` / `.details`, plus `.resources`, `.warnings`, `.verified`, `.ok`). Also public: `validate_graph(objects, root, ...)` and `load_graph(path_or_bytes)`. Codes mirror Extron exactly (`VALID=0`, `MISMATCH_HASH=80085`, `NO_HASH_NO_GUID=80086`), plus two negative repo-local sentinels documented as *not* Extron codes: `UNVERIFIABLE=-1` (a resource whose bytes are not in the package — GC would throw `ArgumentNullException` out of `SequenceEqual`, so there is no honest Extron code) and `UNPARSEABLE=-2`. CLI: `python tools/pkp_validate.py [-v] FILE...`, exit 0 only if every package is Valid **and** every resource was actually hashed.

**Measured while building this**: the comm-sheet PDF is embedded, not external — the brief's open question. Manifest is the child asset named `Manifest` (the serialized `_manifest` field is null in all 9 samples); its `StreamResourceAsset` children carry `.pdf` bytes exactly as `.py` bytes, and `sha256(content) == _resourceHashDict[key]` for all 20 resources across all 9 packages. A stale PDF digest fails with 80085 identically (test [6]).

**Disagreements/uncertainties recorded in the module header, not silently resolved** — 8 numbered gaps, each with "what this file does": (1) the ExtronDH.dat Guid table is a caller-supplied parameter defaulting to *empty*, so an 80086 from this tool is flagged as a prediction; (2) the `"eir"` bypass is tested against **both** the serialized `_filename` and the on-disk name, and only taken when they agree — a one-sided hit becomes a warning and hashing proceeds; (3) non-`byte[]` content → `UNVERIFIABLE`; (4) missing `Manifest` child → Valid per the majority IL reading but `verified=False` + warning; (5) `get_Item` name matching (`_name` → `_defaultName`, multiple matches = warning, hash all); (6) whether `get_Manifest` filters (fails safe); (7) orphan dict keys are inert, informational only; (8) the PDF-hash question, recorded as settled by measurement against the brief's premise.

**Final test output (verbatim, tail):**

So the oracle cannot distinguish "not a driver module" from "a driver module with zero commands" — and `opaque_markers: 0` reads as a clean extraction. Given STATUS.md's finding 14 scored 352 pairs automatically, a `commands_found == 0` guard is worth adding.

On the two real modules it works, mostly:

| module | commands | resolved |
|---|---|---|
| `mod_ross_matrix_RossTalk_v1_1_0_0.py` | 5 | `SalvoRecall` → `'GPI {}\r\n'`, `LoadSet` → `'LOADSET {}\r\n'`, `CustomControl` → `'CC {}{}\r\n'` (params `['Bank']`), `ConnectionStatus` empty, **`MatrixTieCommand` → `'{}'` with slot `OPAQUE:CmdString`** |

**Under-extraction 1 — the important one.** `MatrixTieCommand` is the module's only real command and the oracle loses it entirely. RossTalk's shape is assign-in-both-arms (:38-41), call-after (:42), so `CmdString` is unbound at the call site → one opaque marker.

I verified this is the cause, not a coincidence. Hoisting the `__SetHelper` call into each arm (source otherwise untouched) turns one opaque template into two fully-resolved ones:

```

'XPT D:{} S:{} I:99\r\n'       slots ["qualifier['Output']", "qualifier['Input']"]                        opaque=0
```

And I confirmed the blind spot has never been exercised: across all nine machine-generated modules in `samples/`, the "assign `CmdString` inside an `If` arm, call the helper after the `If`" shape occurs **zero** times, despite those files containing plenty of branching (DSC: 45 `Set`/`Update` methods, 24 `If` nodes; Automate VX: 27 and 25). Extron's generator always emits the helper call inside the branch that built the string. The first hand-written input in the repo hits the gap on its first non-trivial command. The docstring at :617-620 even claims the behaviour it doesn't have ("branch arms get their own env, so an if/else with two different CmdStrings yields two entries") — true only when the *call* is in the arm.

**Under-extraction 2 — format specs are silently discarded.** `render` (:429-438) splits the template on `re.split(r"\{[^{}]*\}", base_str)`, so `{:02}` and `{}` are indistinguishable. RossTalk :47 `'GPI {:02}'.format(int(value))` renders as `'GPI {}\r\n'` and :57 `'CC {}{:02}'` as `'CC {}{}\r\n'`. `GPI 05` and `GPI 5` compare equal in the oracle; on a Ross Ultrix they are different GPI triggers. Scanning all samples for real format specs (`{n:spec}`) finds them in exactly two files: this hand-written module (`{:02}` ×2, i.e. half its `Set` commands) and Tesira :892 (`{2:.1f}`). So this is a pre-existing false-negative class that was near-latent in machine-generated input and becomes prominent in hand-written input.

Both gaps are fixable in `wire_table.py` and neither requires re-deriving anything: merge branch-arm assignments back into the parent env when a name is assigned in every arm (or carry alternatives), and keep the format spec in the rendered canonical string.

    def __init__(self):
        self.ConnectionType = conntype   # :1042, with SerialOverEthernet/SSH folded to 'Ethernet'
        mod.__init__(self)
self.device = devclass()                 # :1044
self.device.Send = self.Send             # :1045
self.device.SendAndWait = self.SendAndWait
self.device.SubscribeStatus = self.__subscriber.SubscribeStatus
self.device.NewStatus = self.__replacement_newstatus
self.device.Update = self.__replacement_update
self.device.Set = self.__replacement_set
self.device.Error = self.__replacement_error
self.device.Discard = self.__replacement_discard      # :1046-1053
```

Each wrapper then builds its own interface object (:1581-1589, :1595-1605, :1611-1621, …) with only `Error`/`Discard`/`Disconnect` overridden. **Consequence: the three transport classes at the bottom of every generated module are dead code under this framework.** The plugin imports `DeviceClass` (:5-6), not `EthernetClass`. That directly touches an assumption in the translator work — the three transport classes are a *GC/ControlScript packaging convention*, not part of the driver contract. A synthesised i20 module needs them to look like a driver; it does not need them to work.

The wrapper also re-exposes the full `DeviceClass` facade — `Set` (:1293), `Update` (:1308), `ReadStatus` (:1323), `SubscribeStatus` (:1335), `Connect` (:1276), `Disconnect` (:1267), `OnConnected`/`OnDisconnected` (:1289-1292) — wrapping each in try/except with `print` + `DebugPrint.Print` + `ProgramLog` and a trace line, and gates sends on `self.device.connectionFlag` for non-serial types (:1201-1204, :1229-1232). That is the API contract the plugin codes against, and it is the same one an Extron module presents. The `#type:switch_mod` comments at plugin :23-25 annotate `parent.switch` as the *DeviceClass* while the runtime object is (on the evidence of `tools.py` sitting in the same folder and providing exactly this surface — `main_switch.py` is not in the sample set) one of these wrappers. The author lies to the type checker to get completion, which is itself the assertion that wrapper and `DeviceClass` are interchangeable.

**Two patterns to copy for the i20:**

1. *Feedback via a second channel.* If the i20's VISCA path gives no unsolicited status, the Ross precedent says: add a second module on a second protocol/port, subscribe to it, and let the plugin present one device upward. TSL's `EthernetClass` defaults `IPPort=5727` (:267) while RossTalk's has no default (:252) — one module per protocol, each carrying its own port convention.
2. *Subscribe-then-force.* `subscribe()` (:62-77) registers callbacks, calls `OnDisconnected()` to force an immediate status publish, then defers `Connect()` behind `@Wait(0.1)` (:70-77) to get out of the construction call chain. Note the three waits are all `0.1` — they fire together, so this is deferral, not staggering, despite reading like staggering. `Timer` is imported at :8 and never used; there is no polling and no `ReadStatus` call anywhere in the plugin. All state flows one way: device → `AddMatchString` → `WriteStatus` → `NewStatus` → plugin closure → `main_switch`.

**Contradicted assumption, stated plainly:** the repo has treated `DeviceClass` + `Commands` + three transports as *the* ControlScript driver shape, and `wire_table.py` encodes that shape as its parser's entry assumption (`tools/wire_table.py:592`, `:603`). The Ross material shows a real deployment where a "driver" is *n* modules plus a plugin, where the transport classes are unused, where one module has no `Set` methods and another has no `Update` methods, and where the wire table for the device is split across two files that the oracle can only read one at a time. Any scorecard built on per-file extraction will mis-measure hand-written drivers in exactly this way.

## What the file actually is

`samples/Custom Module/tools.py` is **not a driver**. It is a 7,644-line general-purpose ControlScript runtime framework — header at `tools.py:47-51`: *Author: Jean-Luc Rioux, Company: Valley Communications, Version 1.6.0.0, 2023-01-02, Minimum Pro Controller FW 3.10* — with a 90-line hand-maintained changelog (`tools.py:52-140`) running from v1.0 to v1.6.0.0. The device drivers in that folder are the two `mod_ross_matrix_*.py` files; `plugin_ross_ultrix.py` is a device-specific translation layer; `tools.py` is the substrate all three run on. So the folder is a complete three-tier hand-built stack: **module (wire) → plugin (semantics) → framework (transport/debug/persistence)**, and *none of it is a `.pkp`*.

30 top-level classes (AST-verified). Grouping:

| lines | classes | role |
|---|---|---|
| 161-590 | `status_report`, `NonvolatileValues`, `ProgramLogSaver`, `DebugFileLogSaver` | JSON persistence to `/NVRAM/`, log rotation with a 90%-storage cap |
| 644-1000 | `DebugServer`, `_PrintWrapper`, `DebugPrint` | a telnet debug server on TCP 1988 (`tools.py:666`), one synthetic "listening port" per wrapped object (`tools.py:894`) |
| 1002-1669 | `__InterfaceWrapper` + 6 transport subclasses | the part that matters here |
| 1670-4435 | 12 `*InterfaceWrapper` classes (Relay, IR, FlexIO, Volume, PoE, SWAC, Tally, Contact, DigitalIO/Input, CircuitBreaker, SWPower) | processor **ports** |
| 4436-6266 | `ProcessorDeviceWrapper`, `SPDeviceWrapper`, `UIDeviceWrapper` | processor/panel **devices** |
| 6313-7644 | `VirtualUI` | synthetic touch panel, multi-panel combine |

## 1. Structure vs Extron's generated modules

**The framework does not contain a `DeviceClass` — it *consumes* one.** `__InterfaceWrapper.__fn_device_init` (`tools.py:1024-1067`) takes the module's `DeviceClass` as a constructor argument (`tools.py:1003`), builds an on-the-fly subclass that sets `ConnectionType` before calling `mod.__init__` (`tools.py:1035-1043`), instantiates it **without any transport base class** (`tools.py:1044`), and then rebinds the contract methods onto the instance:

```
1045  self.device.Send        = self.Send
1046  self.device.SendAndWait = self.SendAndWait
1047  self.__subscriber = self.__ModuleSubscribeWrapper(self.device)
1048  self.device.SubscribeStatus = self.__subscriber.SubscribeStatus
1049  self.device.NewStatus       = self.__replacement_newstatus
1050  self.device.Update          = self.__replacement_update
1051  self.device.Set             = self.__replacement_set
1052  self.device.Error / 1053 .Discard
```

That is the single deepest deviation, and it is unambiguously deliberate. Extron's generator emits *inheritance*: `class EthernetClass(EthernetClientInterface, DeviceClass)` with `DeviceClass.__init__(self)` and the `Models` check inline (`mod_ross_matrix_RossTalk_v1_1_0_0.py:206-224`, `226-247`, `250-272`; shipped `extr_scaler_DSC_12G_HD_A_v1_0_0_0.py:1217`). The author replaces it with *composition + monkeypatching*, and to prove he knows exactly which pieces of the generated tail he is replacing, he reimplements the rest verbatim: the Models-mismatch block (`tools.py:1059-1063` vs `mod_ross_...:212-217`) and the `Error`/`Discard` bodies including the exact `portInfo = 'Host Alias: {0}, Port: {1}'` / `'IP Address/Host: {0}:{1}'` strings (`tools.py:1583-1589`, `1597-1601` vs `mod_ross_...:219-223`, `239-243`). The six transport subclasses `SerialModuleWrapper` / `SerialOverEthernetModuleWrapper` / `EthernetModuleWrapper` / `DanteModuleWrapper` / `SSHModuleWrapper` / `SPIModuleWrapper` (`tools.py:1577, 1591, 1607, 1623, 1639, 1655`) each expose one `Create_Device(...)` with Extron's own parameter list, so the three generated transport classes become *six wrapper classes that work for every module*. Note `SerialOverEthernet` and `SSH` are collapsed to `ConnectionType = 'Ethernet'` under the hood (`tools.py:1038-1041`) — the changelog calls this out at v1.4.1.

**What conforms exactly.** `Set`/`Update` dispatch by `getattr(self, 'Set%s' % command)` is preserved (`tools.py:1194`, `1217`); `ReadStatus`/`WriteStatus` are **not** replaced at all, so the module's own change-detection (`WriteStatus` fires `NewStatus` only when `Status['Live'] != value`, `mod_ross_...:151-157`) survives untouched. The `Commands = {name: {'Parameters': [...], 'Status': {}}}` shape is not just consumed but *reproduced*: all 16 port/device wrappers declare their own `self.Commands` in Extron's exact dict-of-dicts form (`tools.py:1688`, `1850`, `2012`, `2208`, `2485`, `2795`, `3052`, `3273` (Relay), `3494`, …, `4127+`, `4436+`, `5101+`). The author took a contract Extron defines only for *device modules* and applied it to relays, IR ports, PoE and touch panels, so a `RelayInterface` looks like a driver to the debug client.

**The one deliberate contract break.** `__ModuleSubscribeWrapper` (`tools.py:1521-1573`) changes `Method['callback']` from a single callable to a **list**: `Method['callback'].append(callback)` / `= [callback]` (`tools.py:1565-1571`), versus Extron's `Method['callback'] = callback` (`mod_ross_...:114`). This is incompatible with the module's own `NewStatus`, which calls `Method['callback'](command, value, qualifier)` (`mod_ross_...:133`) — a list is not callable. He therefore *must* replace `NewStatus` in the same breath, and does, on the adjacent line (`tools.py:1048-1049`). Paired substitution of two boilerplate methods to add multi-subscriber support is engineering, not sloppiness; the docstring at `tools.py:1512-1519` states the intent ("allows multiple event handlers... in the order that was subscribed").

**Sloppiness, separately, is real and locatable.** `tools.py:1349` reads `self.receiveBuff__receiveBufferCallbackserCallbacks.append(function)` — a botched global rename; `addReceiveBufferCallback` raises `AttributeError` on every call (its sibling `removeReceiveBufferCallback` at 1350-1351 is correct). `ReadStatus` (`tools.py:1323-1334`) returns `value` from outside the `try`, so an exception in the module yields `UnboundLocalError` after the handler already logged — the same class of bug the changelog claims fixed at v1.4.1. `tools.py:7186` is `if action is not 'Changed'` (identity on a literal; works only by CPython interning). This is the pattern of the file: architecture chosen carefully, details unpolished.

## 2. What the author does that the generator does not, and vice versa

**Author only:**
- **Transport-agnostic modules.** One `DeviceClass`, six transports, chosen at `Create_Device` time (`tools.py:1577-1669`) instead of baked into the file's tail.
- **Connection-state gating on Set/Update.** `if self.__interface_type in ['Serial','SPI']: method(...) elif self.device.connectionFlag: method(...)` (`tools.py:1201-1204`, `1229-1232`) — a generated module will happily build and drop a command string into a dead socket.
- **Command pacing.** `time_between_commands` spins a `Timer` that drains a queue one command per tick and yields to `SendAndWait` (`tools.py:1020-1022`, `1069-1078`). Extron's generator has no rate limiter.
- **Auto-reconnect**, retry every 10s with trace/log per attempt (docstring `tools.py:601-602`, `Connect` at `tools.py:1276-1291`).
- **Total exception containment.** Every wrapper entry point is `try/except` → `print` + `DebugPrint.Print` + `ProgramLog`, with a `sys_allowed_flag` fallback (`tools.py:26-29`) for firmware where `import sys, traceback` is blocked (`tools.py:1175-1181`, `1327-1333`, and ~60 more sites). A generated module's `Set` prints `'does not support Set.'` and nothing else.
- **A live wire tap.** Every byte in and out is mirrored to a telnet client and to CSV on the controller (`tools.py:1085-1094`, `__printToLog`/`__printToServer`), plus remote `Set(`/`Update(`/`WriteStatus(` injection parsed out of the debug socket (`tools.py:1369-1465`) — you can drive an unfinished driver from a laptop with no touch panel.
- **Multi-subscriber events**, NVRAM JSON persistence with corrupt-file deletion (`tools.py:310-320`), storage-capped log rotation, and `VirtualUI` (`tools.py:6313-7644`) for testing panel logic with no panel present.
- **Version discipline**: a semver-ish changelog naming the bug fixed in each release (`tools.py:52-140`). Nothing in Extron's generated output carries that.

**Generator only (absent from the hand-written stack):** `__UpdateHelper` and any polling/verbose-mode machinery — the RossTalk module has `__SetHelper` (`mod_ross_...:180-182`, reduced to `self.Debug = True; self.Send(commandstring)`) and **no** `__UpdateHelper` and **no** `Update*` methods at all; the whole driver is write-only plus a connection heartbeat. `Models{}` subclassing is declared but empty in both Ross modules (`:20`). Response parsing is one regex in one of the two modules (`mod_ross_matrix_tsl_3_1:105`). Extron's DSC module ships 30 `AddMatchString` calls and 24 `Update*` methods for 29 commands; the human shipped 1 and 0 for 5. **The human writes only the commands the room needs**, which is the single biggest structural difference between hand-written and generated drivers, and the one that will bite any coverage metric.

## 3. `tools/wire_table.py` on `tools.py` — it under-extracts, three separate ways

Command as given:

```
$ python -c "... wire_table.extract_table(open('samples/Custom Module/tools.py').read(),'tools.py') ..."
0 []
```

**Zero commands, no exception, no warning.** Cause: `_find_main_class` (`tools/wire_table.py:592-597`) returns *the first top-level `ClassDef` in the module*. For `tools.py` that is `status_report` (`tools.py:161`), which has no `self.Commands`. Every other class is never looked at. This is fine on machine-generated modules — `DeviceClass` is always first — and silently wrong on any multi-class file.

The content is there. Extracting each top-level class's source and feeding it to the oracle individually yields **16 tables, 92 commands**:

```
UIDeviceWrapper 34, ProcessorDeviceWrapper 14, SPDeviceWrapper 12, VolumeInterfaceWrapper 6,
PoEInterfaceWrapper 4, FlexIO/IR/SWACReceptacle 3 each, Relay/Contact/Tally/SWPower/
DigitalIO/DigitalInput/CircuitBreaker 2 each, _PrintWrapper 1
```

So the oracle's failure here is *selection*, not parsing. A `--class` argument, or "iterate every class that assigns `self.Commands` and merge/report per class", fixes it. Since the wrapper commands have no `Set*`/`Update*` methods, all 92 come back with empty templates — correctly.

Two further defects, found on the hand-written *drivers* next door, both of which spill onto shipped Extron code:

**(a) `from re import compile` blinds the response side completely.** `_collect_add_match_strings` (`tools/wire_table.py:730-780`) requires the pattern argument to be `ast.Attribute`-`compile` (i.e. `re.compile(...)`). `mod_ross_matrix_tsl_3_1:105` writes `self.AddMatchString(compile(rb'...'), self.__MatchOutputTieStatus, None)` after `from re import compile, search` (`:2`) → `ast.Name` → dropped. Measured: `OutputTieStatus` comes back `responses=[]`; textually patching the import style takes `match_strings_total` from 0 to 1. **This is not a hand-written-code problem.** `samples/Tesira/controlscript/biam_dsp_TesiraSeries_v1_18_3_0.py` — a *shipped Extron module* — uses the same idiom for all **47** of its `AddMatchString` calls, and the oracle reports `match_strings_total: 0, match_strings_unmapped: 0` on it while happily reporting 74 commands. Patched, it goes to 6 (the other 41 build the pattern with `.format(tag).encode()` and are genuinely dynamic — but they too are dropped without being counted). Compare `DSC_12G-HD`, which uses `import re`: `match_strings_total: 30, mapped: 27`. Under the repo's own rule that an unresolvable thing must become a *counted* opaque marker, this is a violation: the drop is invisible, and any per-driver response-coverage number computed over the 312-pair corpus of finding 14 is wrong for every module using this import style.

**(b) `if/else` that joins before the helper call goes opaque.** `SetMatrixTieCommand` (`mod_ross_matrix_RossTalk_v1_1_0_0.py:229-238`) assigns bare `CmdString` in both branches and calls `self.__SetHelper` once *after* the `if`. Result: `('{}', ['OPAQUE:CmdString'])` — both real templates (`XPT D:{} S:{} I:99 L:{}\r\n` and `XPT D:{} S:{} I:99\r\n`) lost. Extron's generator never produces that shape: it emits `<Command>CmdString = ...` **and** the helper call inside the same guarded branch (`extr_scaler_DSC_12G_HD_A_v1_0_0_0.py:105-107`, `223-227`). Isolated with a three-variant probe (left at `tools/out/tmp/wt_probe.py`): single-assign-then-call resolves; call-inside-each-branch resolves to two templates; **assign-in-both-branches-then-call goes opaque**. The variable name is irrelevant. This is a join-point limitation in `_find_helper_calls_in_method`, and hand-written code hits it immediately.

**(c) Minor but misleading:** `Template.opaque` is assigned `resolver.opaque_count` (`tools/wire_table.py:838`, `849`), a **running total for the whole file**, not a per-template count. On the RossTalk module the fully-resolved `SalvoRecall`, `LoadSet` and `CustomControl` all report `opaque=1`, inherited from `MatrixTieCommand`. Anything that thresholds per-template opacity is reading a monotonic counter.

**(d) A hand-written bug the oracle cannot see, by construction:** `SetSalvoRecall` calls `self.__SetHelper('PresetRecall', ...)` (`mod_ross_matrix_RossTalk_v1_1_0_0.py:243`) — a command name that does not exist in `self.Commands`. The oracle keys off the *method* name, so it reports a healthy `SalvoRecall → 'GPI {}\r\n'`. Harmless in this module because the helper ignores its `command` argument (`:180-182`), but it is exactly finding 11's false-positive class, now observed in the wild.

## 4. For the i20, and what it contradicts

**The load-bearing point for finding 13/15.** A programmer facing hardware the vendor does not support did **not** author a `.pkp`. He wrote a plain ControlScript module in Extron's `DeviceClass` shape, dropped it in a Python-mode project, and built framework glue around it. There is no package, no asset tree, no hash dictionary, no `DriverAssetValidator` — and therefore no `80085`. Finding 15's conclusion (the asset tree, not the script, declares the command surface) is confirmed from the other direction: the professional answer to "the vendor doesn't ship a driver" is to leave the packaged-driver path entirely. For the i20 that means the standalone-module form in `experiments/skeleton_i20/` is not the fallback — **it is the shape a working programmer ships**, and the `.pkp` transplant is the harder, validator-gated path taken only when GC's GUI must see the device.

**Directly reusable, and worth copying rather than reinventing:**
- The wrapper pattern itself (`tools.py:1024-1067`): write the i20 module as a bare `DeviceClass` with no transport base, and pick the transport at instantiation. It halves the boilerplate our emitter has to generate (three near-identical tail classes → none) and it is the pattern the local integrator already runs in production.
- `plugin_ross_ultrix.py` as the template for the semantic layer: device-specific arithmetic lives there, not in the module. `setMatrixTieCommand` (`:44-53`) maps a UI concept ("Audio/Video") to `Levels='1-17'` and adds a `+53` output offset before calling `self.dev.Set('MatrixTieCommand', None, {...})`. The i20's reserved-preset auto-switching (finding 13) is exactly this kind of encoding and belongs in a plugin, not in the wire table.
- The connection-gated `Set`/`Update` (`tools.py:1201-1204`) and the command pacer (`tools.py:1069-1078`): both are things our generated modules lack and a camera on a slow TCP socket will need.
- The debug tap (`tools.py:1369-1465`) — remote `Set`/`Update`/`WriteStatus` injection over TCP 1988 — is a ready-made way to exercise a generated i20 module against real hardware without building a UI.

**What it contradicts / qualifies:**
1. The oracle's opacity accounting is not sound in the response direction. `match_strings_total: 0` currently reads as "this driver has no response patterns", and it is produced by a shipped Extron module. Fix `_collect_add_match_strings` to accept `ast.Name`-`compile` and to count dropped dynamic patterns, then re-run finding 14's response-side numbers.
2. "Acceptance is the wire-string table" assumes there is one class to extract it from. It returns `0` — not an error — on any file that is not a single-`DeviceClass` module, which is the shape of most hand-written code. `extract_table` should raise or report per-class when the first class carries no `Commands`.
3. Hand-written drivers are *deliberately partial*: 5 commands, no `Update*`, one match string, for a device with a large API. Scoring a generated i20 module against "what a human would write" will overstate the gap; scoring against "what the room needs" has no oracle at all.
4. Style assumptions to note before generating: zero f-strings and zero variable annotations in 7,644 lines (AST-verified) — everything is `.format()` and `:'str'` / `#type:` comments, consistent with the declared FW 3.10 floor. Emit the same dialect.
